name: Nanohybrid composite fillings

lead: Nanohybrid composites are tooth-coloured filling materials in which resin is loaded with glass or silica particles of mixed sizes, including nano-scale ones. Dentists use them to repair cavities, chips and worn edges so the repair matches the surrounding tooth.

Because shades can be matched closely and the surface polishes well, the result is a repair that is hard to see, especially on front teeth. Dental reference material describes the appearance as far superior to silver amalgam, with typical lifespans of around ten years when placed well.

paras: A dentist removes decay or damaged tooth, selects a shade, places the composite in layers, hardens each layer with a curing light, then shapes and polishes it. The tooth has to stay dry throughout, which is why technique matters. The same material is used for chip repair, closing small gaps and reshaping edges (bonding).

Reported drawbacks include shrinkage during hardening, which can leave a gap at the edge and lead to new decay, chipping in large restorations and a longer, costlier visit than amalgam. Minor defects can often be repaired rather than replaced. Material choice is made by the treating dentist.

chain: Matches resin shade to the surrounding tooth
Repaired chips or cavities look like natural enamel
angle.text: A dentist fills or reshapes the tooth with resin matched to its colour, so the repair is hard to see. Front-tooth chips, worn edges and small gaps can be restored in a single visit.

lead: Nanohybrid composites are a class of dental composite resin: a plastic matrix filled with a blend of particle sizes that includes nano-scale particles. They are used for tooth-coloured fillings and cosmetic bonding. [1]

For appearance, the draw is shade matching and polish. Composites come in a wide range of tooth shades and can be matched closely to existing teeth, which matters most for front teeth, and the nano-scale filler lets surfaces polish to a smooth finish. [1]
Properly placed composite restorations can last ten years or more, with annual failure rates of roughly 1 to 3 percent reported for posterior fillings in a 2012 review. [1]
infobox: Mixed micro- and nano-scale glass/silica particles

paras: Composite resins are classed by filler particle size: macrofilled, microfilled, hybrid and nanofilled. Hybrids combine particle sizes at about 75 to 85 percent filler by weight and are stronger than microfilled types. Nanofilled materials use particles of about 20 to 70 nm, are strong, wear-resistant and polish easily, but are harder to adapt to cavity margins. Nanohybrids blend nano particles with larger ones to balance polish and strength. [1]

Composites are available in many shades and can be closely matched to natural teeth, particularly in anterior teeth, and their appearance is described as far superior to amalgam. Microfilled and nanofilled resins polish most easily, with aluminium oxide discs giving a desirable finish. Darker shades need longer curing. [1]

A 2012 review found annual failure rates of 1 to 3 percent for posterior composites, compared with about 3 percent for amalgam in a 2004 review. Secondary caries is the main reason for failure, and one study of 1,748 restorations found 3.5 times the secondary caries risk with composite versus amalgam. Polymerization shrinkage can cause microleakage, the material is technique-sensitive because the tooth must stay dry, and it often costs more with limited insurance cover. Minor defects can usually be repaired. [1]

No studies found for the nanohybrid category in this wiki's source set; the wider dental-composite literature summarised above reports annual failure rates of 1 to 3 percent for posterior composites. [1]
